preamble: The shift from the full vowel [æ] to the mid-central vowel [ə] (schwa) is a classic case of vowel reduction. In stress-timed English, /æ/ in a syllable that loses stress centralizes to [ə], producing systematic alternations in derivationally related words. Because few languages that reduce unstressed vowels to schwa also have a distinct /æ/, the pattern is well documented chiefly from English.

examples.note: When stress shifts to the second syllable, the first-syllable [æ] reduces to [ə].
The unstressed second element of the compound reduces [æ] to [ə].

sources: Ladefoged, P. & Johnson, K. (2015). A Course in Phonetics (7th ed.). Cengage Learning. https://mitpressbookstore.mit.edu/book/9781285463407
context: In unstressed syllables in English; conditioned by stress placement
allophones_note: English vowel reduction: /æ/ surfaces as [ə] when unstressed
